item.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents pay without seeing your card details
item.description: OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a way for its Dots agents to pay for purchases on a user's behalf without seeing the user's actual card details. Users add a card once and approve each purchase with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint, after which the payment network issues a token in place of the real card number. The wallet starts with ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US, built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and OpenAI has published a Commerce Partner Playbook to help businesses accept agent payments. Why it matters for tech: Agent-led shopping only works if payments are safe and merchants can accept them, so a wallet built on existing card rails is the missing piece for agentic commerce.

item.title: Anthropic opens a private beta for self-hosted Claude Managed Agents
item.description: Anthropic has opened a private beta of self-hosted Claude Managed Agents, letting companies run the whole agent service inside their own cloud or data centre. The harness, sandboxes, credentials and session history all run on the customer's infrastructure, while model calls still go to a provider the customer chooses, such as Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry. Access is limited to eligible organisations through their Anthropic account team, and the server licence requires customers to roll back a version within eight hours of a safety notice. Why it matters for tech: Teams that want long-running agents working on internal code can now keep the control plane behind their own security perimeter instead of handing it to a vendor.

item.title: llama.cpp reaches 1.0 with a stability promise for local AI builders
item.description: The llama.cpp project has released version 1.0.0 of its libraries, committing to semantic versioning so that breaking changes to the public C API will only arrive with major version bumps. The project, which lets developers run multimodal language models on hardware from consumer laptops to enterprise servers, now supports more than 150 model architecture variants. The release also covers ggml 1.0.0, the tensor library underneath it. Why it matters for tech: Local and private AI products depend on llama.cpp, so a stable API gives their builders a firmer foundation to build on.

item.title: Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM simulate drug binding across 12,000 atoms
item.description: A collaboration between Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM has run a hybrid quantum-classical simulation of full protein-ligand complexes exceeding 12,000 atoms, described as the largest such calculation to date. The team paired two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors with three supercomputers, collecting 3.0 billion measurement shots across 21,006 circuits, and reported up to a 210-fold improvement in fragment energy accuracy over earlier quantum-embedding benchmarks. The work, detailed in a preprint, produced a binding energy prediction for a T4-lysozyme complex. Why it matters for tech: Drug binding predictions at this scale move quantum computing closer to real pharmaceutical work, where accurate energies decide which molecules advance.

item.title: A cheaper way to hunt for diamond qubits
item.description: A researcher at the US Department of Energy's Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory has developed a method that cuts the cost of modelling quantum defects in diamond, by treating a cluster of just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect as a separate molecule. The approach, published in ACS Central Science, already identified promising new qubit candidates involving boron and oxygen defects, which emit ultraviolet and blue light respectively, unlike the well-known nitrogen-vacancy centre that emits red. Because each defect type responds to different light, several kinds could be combined in one device and addressed independently. Why it matters for tech: Cheaper screening of diamond defects widens the search for qubits that work at room temperature, which would simplify quantum hardware.

item.title: Google Cloud brings agentic HPC to SC26
item.description: Google Cloud has set out its agentic high-performance computing plans for the SC26 supercomputing conference, centred on reusable agent skills that teach AI agents to build and run HPC workloads through Cluster Toolkit blueprints. The skills validate quotas and capacity before deploying a cluster, guide domain work such as fluid dynamics and life-science pipelines, and operate inside IAM and budget guardrails. The company is also showing AlphaEvolve on Cloud Batch for evolving code at scale, and new hardware including A5X instances on NVIDIA Vera Rubin and 8th generation TPUs. Why it matters for tech: Scientific teams are asking agents to run supercomputing workloads, so packaging HPC expertise into skills keeps those agents from misconfiguring expensive infrastructure.

item.title: Check Point zero-day chained with PHP2Shell to wipe VMware hosts
item.description: Check Point has released emergency hotfixes for a zero-day privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039, that attackers have exploited against a couple of dozen customers since late October. Attackers first entered through Mobile Access portals using the PHP2Shell flaws, then used the flaw to run commands as root, installed the TSGA backdoor, and in an early wave wiped VMware ESXi hosts. The company advises customers who cannot patch immediately to stop the DynamicCLI daemon as a temporary mitigation. Why it matters for tech: A chained portal flaw plus a root escalation shows how one unpatched gateway can become a route to destructive attacks on virtualisation hosts.

item.title: FBI says North Korean hackers stole over $400 million in deepfake video call scheme
item.description: The FBI says North Korean hackers stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over 18 months through a scheme it calls FaceStealer, which lures targets into fake video meetings that play recorded webcam footage of people they trust. Once on the call, victims are told of a fake audio fault and sent a link that installs malware to steal wallets and credentials. US authorities seized the cloud infrastructure behind the scheme and more than 900 recorded victim videos, and the Justice Department separately won court approval to seize or restrain over $1.2 billion stolen from Binance by a different North Korean group. Why it matters for tech: The scheme turns a victim's own face into the lure for the next target, so verifying meeting invitations through a second channel matters more than ever.

item.title: Operation Endgame seizes servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC
item.description: An international police operation has taken down servers behind the Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC malware tools, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains and about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims. Gootloader spread through fake legal documents on hacked websites and was used in ransomware attacks, while CastleRAT gave attackers remote control of infected machines and StealC stole passwords. Dutch police have loaded data stolen by CastleRAT into their Check your hack service so people can see if their email address was affected. Why it matters for tech: Taking down the loaders and stealers that feed ransomware cuts off the access brokers' supply chain, even when no arrests are announced.

item.title: Trezor confirms hardware implants in three wallets and cuts reseller network
item.description: Trezor has confirmed that three Safe 5 hardware wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained hidden circuit boards designed to steal recovery phrases and send them to attackers over a mobile network. The company released firmware 2.13.1 on November 11, which stops the implants from capturing anything on screen, and says no affected customer has reported losing funds. Trezor has also cut its global reseller network by about 80 percent and is offering replacement devices to anyone who bought a wallet from CryptoBilis since March 2026. Why it matters for tech: A hardware wallet is only as trustworthy as its supply chain, so a tampered device shows why buying from authorised sellers matters.

item.title: Atom Computing finalises $100 million Commerce Department award
item.description: Atom Computing has signed an agreement for up to $100 million with the US Department of Commerce to accelerate research and development of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers built on neutral atoms. The award, made under the CHIPS and Science Act, follows a letter of intent announced earlier in 2026 and will fund in-house technology work, expanded engineering and testing infrastructure, and supply chain collaboration. Atom also recently advanced to Stage C of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, with potential funding of up to $300 million. Why it matters for tech: Federal funding at this scale signals that neutral-atom quantum computing is now treated as strategic infrastructure, not just research.

item.title: Operation TorNado arrests 354 in global dark web crackdown
item.description: Police in 14 countries have arrested 354 people and seized more than $234 million in cash and virtual currencies in Operation TorNado, a coordinated action against vendors and buyers on five dark web marketplaces that had already been seized by law enforcement. The operation, which ran from May 2025 to October 2026, also seized about 5.7 metric tons of illicit drugs, 209 firearms and 38 pill presses. The US Justice Department, which announced the results with Europol, said 132 of the arrests were in the United States. Why it matters for tech: Seized marketplaces keep producing leads, so each takedown feeds the next round of arrests rather than ending the trade.

item.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster model built for agentic coding work
item.description: Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a model aimed at everyday coding and multi-step agent workflows rather than long-horizon reasoning, which stays with the Carbon and Argon models. Hydrogen runs across the Gemini API, AI Studio, the Gemini app and Google Search, with a 1 million token context window priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. On Terminal-Bench 4.1 it scored 57%, against 18.2% for Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Google says it completes tasks about 2.5 times faster at its default setting. Why it matters for tech: A cheaper, quicker execution model changes the economics of running agents all day, since most agent work is routine execution rather than deep reasoning.

item.title: Google opens preorders for Gemini smartglasses starting at $395
item.description: Google has opened preorders for its first Gemini-powered smartglasses, built with Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with shipping and store availability from December 10. The glasses have no in-lens display; wearers talk to Gemini by voice, use touch controls, or use a 12 megapixel camera. Warby Parker frames start at $395 in the US and Gentle Monster styles at $449, and Google says the camera has an always-on recording light, a physical off switch, no livestreaming and no real-time face recognition. Why it matters for tech: Glasses put an AI assistant on the face rather than in the hand, so the privacy controls Google ships with them set the pattern other makers will be judged against.

item.title: PsiQuantum and AMD widen their partnership to build the classical side of fault-tolerant quantum computers
item.description: PsiQuantum and AMD have expanded their partnership to co-design the computing infrastructure for utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum machines and the hybrid workloads that mix quantum, high-performance and AI computing. The work moves beyond AMD Versal FPGAs to Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs and the ROCm software stack, paired with PsiQuantum's silicon photonics platform, and AMD also plans an equity investment in PsiQuantum. The first focus is pharmaceutical research and drug discovery, and the companies will share more at the SC26 conference in Chicago from November 15 to 20. Why it matters for tech: Fault-tolerant machines will need as much classical computing around them as quantum hardware inside, so chipmakers are now part of the quantum build.

item.title: Qunova's hybrid method matches the best classical result on a hard chemistry problem
item.description: Qunova Computing says its HI-VQE algorithm reached chemical accuracy in an 80-qubit simulation of the 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur cluster, using an IBM Quantum System Two machine at RIKEN alongside the Fugaku supercomputer. Its ground-state energy estimate of minus 327.2482 Hartree agreed within chemical accuracy with the leading classical reference, calculated by the Density Matrix Renormalization Group method at minus 327.2471 Hartree. The workflow also used about 300 times fewer Fugaku node-hours than a previously published sample-based quantum diagonalization approach on the same molecule. Why it matters for tech: A quantum workflow that agrees with the reference classical calculation on a benchmark molecule gives chemists a reason to trust hybrid methods for real design questions.

item.title: AWS upgrades its AgentCore runtime for faster, cheaper agent sessions
item.description: Amazon Web Services has released a new version of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, the managed layer that runs AI agents in isolated Firecracker micro virtual machines. Sessions now start up to 15 times faster and scale to four times more compute, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of memory, while idle sessions scale to zero and reclaim memory within minutes. Agents can also mount storage such as an S3 bucket inside the session boundary, so data stays under the same controls as the compute. Why it matters for tech: Agents that run for hours need isolation that does not tax every minute of waiting, and this release ties billing and storage to how agents actually work.

item.title: Chainguard defends shipping PHP patches six hours before the agreed release time
item.description: Chainguard has defended its decision to publish patched PHP container images at 07:41 UTC on October 21, six hours and 19 minutes before the agreed 14:00 UTC coordinated release for the critical PHP2Shell flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Chief technology officer Matt Moore told KubeCon that attackers already had a head start, pointing to leaked vulnerability details, a mistakenly published proof-of-concept video, a honeypot exploitation attempt reported by Amazon on October 17, and attack traffic seen by Cloudflare. PHP said it found no working public exploit at release time, and CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26. Why it matters for tech: Coordinated disclosure only works when everyone holds the line, so an early release by one vendor forces the whole industry to rethink how embargoes are enforced.

item.title: Apache patches a critical HTTP/2 flaw that allows remote code execution
item.description: The Apache Software Foundation has fixed a critical race condition in the mod_http2 module of Apache HTTP Server, tracked as CVE-2026-119618, which an unauthenticated attacker could exploit to gain remote code execution. The flaw affects HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner and Google Cloud's Vulnerability Research teams. Cloud security company Wiz reports that 64% of cloud environments hold vulnerable resources, though the flaw needs HTTP/2 enabled, which is off by default, and no public exploit is known. Why it matters for tech: Apache still serves about one in five websites, so a remotely exploitable flaw in its HTTP/2 code is a patch-now item for anyone running it.

item.title: New SignDrop zero-day turns a Windows security mitigation into a privilege escalation
item.description: Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri has disclosed SignDrop, a Windows zero-day that abuses the Common Log File System mitigations Microsoft added in October 2025. The flaw lets an attacker trick a privileged process, such as an antivirus engine, into creating an authentication file with SYSTEM privileges, which can then be used to turn off antivirus and endpoint protection. Naceri tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, estimates 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable, and says there is no fix yet except waiting for a Microsoft patch. Why it matters for tech: A defence that can be turned against itself is a reminder that mitigations need their own review, and defenders cannot patch this one yet.

item.title: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigns; finance chief Colette Kress takes over on an interim basis
item.description: Nvidia has announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of the board, effective immediately, ending 33 years as chief executive of the company he co-founded in 1993. The announcement gave no reason for the departure, which followed days of reports about Huang's personal conduct and a board investigation, while chief financial officer Colette Kress takes over as interim chief executive and the board searches for a permanent successor. The board also named longtime director Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, and Nvidia confirmed its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results will still be reported on November 17 as scheduled. Why it matters for tech: A change at the top of the chipmaker at the centre of the AI buildout will shape chip supply, pricing and US export policy debates.

item.title: Q-CTRL raises $290 million and becomes the quantum sector's newest unicorn
item.description: Q-CTRL has raised US$290 million in a Series C round led by Salesforce Ventures, with participation from Bullhound Capital and Affinity Partners, reaching unicorn status. The oversubscribed round was expanded twice to meet investor demand, and the company says it is the largest fundraise for a software-focused quantum business. Q-CTRL plans to use the money to expand globally, strengthen its AI-powered quantum software, and scale customer programs in finance, energy, autonomy and aerospace, including its Ironstone Opal navigation system that works without GPS. Why it matters for tech: Private money is concentrating on the software layer that makes quantum hardware usable, and a round of this size signals where investors expect value to sit.

item.title: Microsoft 365 outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and Copilot worldwide
item.description: Microsoft is investigating a widespread Microsoft 365 outage that began on Thursday at 1:26 PM ET and left customers unable to connect to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot and Defender XDR. Microsoft said the disruption was caused by servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable, which strained the remaining infrastructure, and it has paused deployments, redistributed traffic and begun restarting servers. By Thursday evening Microsoft reported limited recovery after returning some servers to service, but had not confirmed when services would be fully restored. Why it matters for tech: A single outage that takes out mail, chat and AI assistance at once shows how much daily work now depends on one provider's infrastructure.

item.title: Blacklisted Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite US export controls
item.description: A Reuters investigation of procurement records found that Northwestern Polytechnical University in China bought two Nvidia H200 AI chips for 874,700 yuan, about $123,000, on October 21, through Chinese supplier Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia. The university has been on the US Entity List since 2001 over missile-proliferation and military research concerns, and Reuters reviewed 26 records showing Chinese institutions buying restricted Nvidia chips or renting computing capacity through domestic suppliers. The US has allowed some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis since January, with safeguards against blacklisted and military end users, and Nvidia, the university and the US Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Why it matters for tech: The purchase shows how export controls are tested in practice, through intermediaries and rentals, and the gap between the rules and enforcement is now part of the policy debate.

item.title: Google DeepMind launches AlphaGenome 2 to predict DNA effects in single cell types
item.description: Google DeepMind has announced AlphaGenome 2, a DNA sequence model that predicts how genetic variants affect specific human cell types rather than broad tissue averages. Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, it identified nearly twice as many causal variants on a single-cell immune dataset, 30% against 16% for the original model. The model is available now for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research. Why it matters for tech: Cell-level variant prediction helps researchers connect disease-linked DNA changes to the exact cells where they act, which broad tissue models miss.

item.title: Google launches Gemini Decisions API for fast yes or no and scoring calls
item.description: Google has introduced the Gemini Decisions API, powered by its new Gemini Decision 1 model, which scores up to 1,000 yes or no, multiple choice and rubric questions against one multimodal input in a single pass. It returns probabilities and confidence scores with 150 to 250 milliseconds of end-to-end latency, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens with no output tokens billed. The API is available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, and Google already uses it for model routing, design iteration and safety checks on tools. Why it matters for tech: Scoring options instead of generating text makes routine agent decisions such as routing, policy checks and grading faster and cheaper, and the confidence scores let code send uncertain cases to a human.

item.title: IBM details Nighthawk r3 chip and a 1,040-qubit system for 2027
item.description: IBM has announced Nighthawk r3, a processor designed to run 10,000 quantum operations across 520 programmable qubits, with 2,034 physical qubits in total. IBM plans to link two r3 processors into a single 1,040-qubit system in 2027, using chip to chip interconnects it has already demonstrated. The current Nighthawk r2 runs up to 100,000 samples a second and more than 7,500 operations on 120 qubits, and partners have run 34 billion circuits on it so far. Why it matters for tech: Linking processors with chip to chip interconnects is IBM's route to larger systems without building one giant chip, and sample speed decides whether heavy workloads finish in practical time.

item.title: Rigetti reports third-quarter revenue of $1.4 million and a 99.5% fidelity milestone
item.description: Rigetti reported third-quarter revenue of $1.4 million, with nine-month revenue of $10.9 million, up about 110% on a year earlier, and an operating loss of $33.2 million. The company ended the quarter with $497.1 million in cash and investments and no debt. Its Cepheus-1-108Q system reached 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity, Rigetti signed a definitive agreement for up to $100 million from the US Department of Commerce under the CHIPS Act, and it targets a 300-plus-qubit system at about 99.7% fidelity by mid-2028. Why it matters for tech: The fidelity figure and the federal award show a small quantum hardware maker funding its roadmap from both sales growth and government research money.

item.title: AWS ships a local emulator that runs AWS APIs on your laptop
item.description: AWS Emulator is generally available: it runs on the laptop and answers AWS CLI, SDK and coding-agent calls over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs, with no additional service fee. It is built in Rust from the AWS API models, and an embedded mode runs inside test processes for the Rust SDK. AWS publishes per-service fidelity scores showing how closely the emulator matches real AWS, and an unimplemented operation returns an error instead of silently passing. Why it matters for tech: Developers and coding agents can test AWS calls without deploying, which shortens the loop for agent-built cloud code, though the emulator does not evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does.

item.title: NVIDIA hands OpenShell, its agent security runtime, to the CNCF
item.description: NVIDIA has donated OpenShell, its open-source runtime for securing and governing AI agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, where it joins as a Sandbox project. OpenShell runs an agent inside a sandbox and enforces policy on the files, networks, credentials and model endpoints the agent can reach, using Cedar as its policy language. The donation was announced at KubeCon North America, the project lists about 380 contributing organisations, and Red Hat, Docker and Canonical are among its core contributors. Why it matters for tech: As agents run longer tasks with real credentials, the controls around them become infrastructure, and neutral governance is meant to speed adoption across clouds and tools.

item.description: Maersk has confirmed that a threat actor breached a local legacy system from its acquired LF Logistics arm and stole data. The WhiteArmor ransomware gang claims about 100GB of data and demands $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. Maersk says the incident is isolated to that system, current evidence shows no sensitive data has been disclosed, and operations are unaffected. Why it matters for tech: The breach hit a system inherited through acquisition, which is a reminder that acquired infrastructure carries its own exposure long after the deal closes.

item.title: More than 35,000 Grok-built apps found open online, some leaking confidential data
item.description: Security researchers at Claroc found 37,571 Grok-built apps online, of which 35,578 were open to anyone without signing in. About one in ten contained internal business or personal data, and roughly 2% of the open apps held material rated high or critical. Twenty-four of the apps were built by staff at X and SpaceX, including a confidential sales onboarding plan, and the company has since taken those staff apps down. Why it matters for tech: Apps built by typing a description inherit the builder's sharing default, so a tool meant for quick prototypes can quietly publish internal data.

item.title: CISA adds an exploited Cisco BroadWorks flaw to its must-patch list
item.description: CISA has added CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity flaw in Cisco BroadWorks that lets remote attackers read sensitive configuration, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Federal civilian agencies must patch by November 24, and CISA urges private organisations to prioritise it too. Cisco patched the flaw in August, and threat researchers report it was exploited with help from a jailbroken AI model in attacks on a European telecom provider. Why it matters for tech: A patched flaw becomes urgent once exploitation is confirmed, and the reported AI-assisted attack shows how quickly a known bug can be turned into a live intrusion.

item.description: TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI, with its board approving the plans. Up to $500 million would go into OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors, and $500 million into Anthropic common shares at the price of its expected public listing. TSMC manufactures most of NVIDIA's AI data-centre chips and most of Apple's custom chips, while Anthropic and OpenAI buy large volumes of TSMC-made hardware for their data-centre projects. Why it matters for tech: A chipmaker taking stakes in the AI developers that buy its hardware ties supplier and buyer together, and analysts warn this kind of circular financing makes real demand for AI hardware harder to read.

item.title: US quantum commission warns industrial gaps threaten the long-term lead
item.description: The Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy, convened by the Special Competitive Studies Project and co-chaired by Senators Todd Young and Ben Ray Luján, has published its preliminary strategy report, Defining the American Quantum Era. The report puts China's public quantum funding at about $3 billion a year against about $1 billion in the United States, and US cleanroom construction at $800 to $1,000 per square foot against about $150 in China. It recommends shared fabrication access, securing cryogenics and helium-3 supply lines, and faster migration to post-quantum cryptography, with a final report planned for spring 2027. Why it matters for tech: The report frames quantum leadership as an industrial problem of factories, supply chains and funding, not only a research race, and its recommendations point at federal action on manufacturing and standards.

item.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Carbon with an agent swarm for coding
item.description: Google has made Gemini 4 Carbon publicly available to Gemini app users and to developers through the Gemini API, AI Studio and Vertex AI, after an earlier limited release for cybersecurity work. The model is aimed at agentic coding, including building apps and prototypes and debugging code. Google cites 87.9% on SWE-Bench Verified, against 81% for the previous Gemini 4 Argon, and says one master agent can coordinate up to 10,000 agents that plan, work in parallel and check each other's work. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens. Why it matters for tech: A coding model that coordinates large agent teams changes how much of a build can be handed to agents at once, and the published benchmark figures give teams a concrete basis for comparing it with the previous release.

item.title: Quantinuum and RIKEN complete the Reimei upgrade to the H2 system
item.description: Quantinuum and RIKEN have completed the upgrade of the Reimei quantum computer at RIKEN to Quantinuum's System Model H2, and expanded their partnership around quantum-AI hybrid supercomputing in Japan. The upgraded machine sits alongside RIKEN's Fugaku supercomputer and the ROQUO GPU system, and the partners have started two research projects on it, one training an AI model on quantum data for magnetism simulations and one simulating a light-absorbing biomolecule. Under a separate agreement with SoftBank, the partners will study connecting quantum computers directly with AI data centres in Japan. Why it matters for tech: A working three-way hybrid of quantum, supercomputing and AI hardware gives researchers a live platform for testing whether quantum-generated data improves AI models for materials and biology.

item.title: Xanadu and HyperLight cut photonic switch loss to 7 millidecibels
item.description: Xanadu and HyperLight have reported an optical switch insertion loss of 7 millidecibels using thin-film lithium niobate technology, down from 20 millidecibels in their previous result in 2025. Lower switch loss reduces the degradation of quantum signals as they pass through the switches that route light in a photonic quantum computer. The result was demonstrated on HyperLight's thin-film lithium niobate chiplet platform, which the companies describe as a high-volume wafer manufacturing line. Why it matters for tech: Switch loss is one of the physical limits on scaling photonic quantum computers, so a measured drop of nearly two-thirds changes the overhead budget for larger machines built on this platform.

item.description: Canonical has opened a public preview of Ubuntu Core 26 images for Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, bringing its immutable Ubuntu variant to public cloud marketplaces. Ubuntu Core builds systems from strictly confined snap packages and delivers updates as complete, auditable revisions with rollback, aiming to stop cloud virtual machines drifting from their original configuration. item.title: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixes 1,235 flaws, including an exploited Outlook zero-day
item.description: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday addresses 1,235 vulnerabilities, including 66 rated Critical, with one actively exploited zero-day in Outlook. The zero-day, CVE-2026-124194, is a spoofing flaw in which opening a specially crafted message file can make Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, disclosing the user's NTLMv2 hash. Microsoft rates the flaw Moderate with a CVSS score of 6.5, and CISA added it to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalog on November 10 with a November 24 patching deadline for federal agencies. Why it matters for tech: A single crafted message file can expose credentials used to impersonate a user, so the fix matters for any organisation running Outlook, and the federal deadline sets the pace for patching.

item.title: Attackers exploit a Xen Orchestra authentication bypass to seize virtualisation hosts
item.description: Vates has warned that a critical authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra, tracked as VSA-2026-062, is being actively exploited in the wild. A specially crafted cookie can bypass login and give an attacker administrative actions, leading to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full takeover of an XCP-ng node as root. Vates linked the activity to an IP address previously flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control server. Fixed versions are Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0, and xo-server 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. Why it matters for tech: Xen Orchestra manages virtual machines and server pools, so a login bypass on an internet-facing instance hands an attacker the control plane for the hosts behind it.

item.title: SAP patches four maximum-severity flaws, including two that allow remote code execution
item.description: SAP's November Security Patch Day addresses 38 new vulnerabilities, nine of them rated Critical, with four carrying the maximum CVSS score of 10.0. The four cover a SAML assertion verification bypass in NetWeaver AS ABAP, memory corruption in the Internet Communication Manager, a default access-control setting in SAP Gateway, and a heap overflow in SAP Web Dispatcher. SAP has not reported active exploitation of the four, and none of them appears in CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities catalog. Why it matters for tech: Four maximum-severity flaws in core SAP systems, two of them leading to remote code execution, make patching a priority this week for teams running SAP, even with no exploitation reported yet.

item.title: SSHole flaw lets attackers bypass login on some Linux systems
item.description: A flaw named SSHole allows authentication bypass in OpenSSH on certain Linux systems built on musl, including Alpine, for accounts whose password hash is the single character "*". An oversized password makes musl return "*", which OpenSSH then treats as a match. Exploitation began on November 5, the day a proof of concept appeared, and OpenSSH 10.6p2 was released the same day as the fix. GreyNoise recorded the first successful exploitation on November 7, with 16 successful chains from 6 source IP addresses. Why it matters for tech: The flaw turns a password length check into a login bypass on affected systems, so administrators running musl-based Linux need the patched OpenSSH version rather than relying on password strength.

item.description: Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision found two weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA encryption, a key size the industry retired years ago. In a sandbox test, the agents reproduced a signature forgery on a solved benchmark key using 3.5 times less CPU time, and a new algorithm improved on the previous best method by roughly 1,600 times in theoretical estimates for short fingerprints, while a second result cuts the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30 times. DeepMind states modern 2048-bit and larger keys are unaffected and no live systems were touched. Why it matters for tech: AI agents are now doing original cryptanalysis in weeks, so hardness assumptions need continuous re-testing rather than being treated as fixed.

item.title: Oxford team simulates Aharonov-Bohm effect with two trapped ions
item.description: Researchers at the University of Oxford have simulated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer, in a study published in Nature Physics. Two trapped ions formed a loop with two paths, and entangling the qubits that encode the magnetic flux changed whether a particle could tunnel between sites. When the entangled qubits encoded a nonzero flux, the two paths cancelled out and tunnelling stopped entirely, showing the simulation captures how flux affects particle motion. Why it matters for tech: Simulating gauge theories with matter and flux together moves quantum simulation closer to the physics behind particle interactions and exotic materials.

item.title: AI assisted proof settles a 2008 question about quantum speedups
item.description: A proof by David Turturean of Physical Superintelligence has settled the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008, which asks when quantum computers can gain dramatic advantages over classical machines. The proof shows that for yes or no questions on most randomly generated inputs, a classical algorithm can estimate a quantum algorithm’s answer without needing vastly more reads of the input, so large speedups need structure in the problem. The proof was found by an AI research system using a non public Anthropic model on the third day of a run, then checked in the Lean proof assistant and reviewed by researchers. Why it matters for tech: It draws a clearer line around where quantum advantage can come from, pointing algorithm research toward problems with structure worth exploiting.

item.title: OpenSSH ships emergency fix for a flaw that let long passwords bypass login on Alpine Linux
item.description: OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 to fix a critical flaw in which a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long could log in to accounts with no password set, such as key only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers. The flaw affects systems where the server checks passwords without PAM, which is how Alpine's openssh-server package is built. Alpine published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16, and no attacks using the flaw have been reported. Why it matters for tech: A password check that accepts the wrong input is a serious failure, and Alpine's wide use in containers makes fast patching matter.

item.description: Researchers have produced experimental support for the theoretical basis of topological quantum computing, an approach that stores information in special quantum states expected to be more resistant to local disturbances. Why it matters for tech: If topological approaches hold up, they could reduce the error correction burden that dominates quantum hardware design today.

item.title: Russia plans underground data centres after Ukrainian drone strikes

Why it matters for tech: The conflict is directly reshaping where and how a major state builds and protects its data centre capacity.
